page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard1.16 is a general-purpose virtual machine configuration belonging to the first-generation Standard instance family. It is equipped with 16 physical cores and 32 vCPUs sourced from an Intel Xeon E5-2699 v3 processor clocked at 2.3 GHz, utilizing hyper-threading at two threads per core. Memory allocation totals 112.0 GB of RAM, which equates to 3.5 GB of memory per allocated vCPU.

The instance relies on the x86_64 architecture and operates with dedicated CPU resource allocations. It includes no bundled local storage, meaning all persistent data storage must be attached via remote block volumes or network-attached solutions. There are no discrete hardware accelerators or GPUs integrated into the configuration. Network access includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Because the underlying Intel Xeon processor represents an earlier generation of server silicon, raw per-core performance is lower than modern alternatives. However, the 32-vCPU and 112.0 GB memory density provides stable multi-threaded execution for legacy enterprise software, internal services, general web serving, application middleware, and continuous integration pipelines that do not demand cutting-edge instructions or local NVMe storage.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard1.16 is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the x86_64 architecture, providing 32 vCPUs across 16 physical cores powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2699 v3 processor running at 2.3 GHz. The instance delivers a dedicated CPU allocation accompanied by 112.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced profile of 3.5 GB of RAM per vCPU. This configuration does not include local disk storage, requiring external block storage for data persistence, and operates without discrete GPU acceleration. Network provisioning comes with one complimentary public IPv4 address. Operating on legacy Intel Xeon hardware, VM.Standard1.16 is suited for multi-threaded enterprise services, middle-tier application hosting, standard web servers, and batch processing workloads that do not rely on modern vector instruction sets or extreme single-threaded compute performance.
